newsitem.title: UK: Hong Kong faces rosy future - investors.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong faces rosy future - investors.

text.p: The sun may be setting on the British Empire in Hong Kong in a month's time but foreign investors foresee a rosy future under China.
"I think it will continue to be a real winner," said Richard Farrell of Guinness Flight Hambro.
For he like other fund managers echoes the market view that Hong Kong under new management is still a sound bet.

"The combination of southern China taken with Hong Kong is potentially the jewel in the crown of Asia," he said of the teeming metropolis being handed back to Beijing on June 30 after 156 years of British rule.

Fund managers worry about soaring Hong Kong property prices as a damper on economic growth and fear outside factors like U.S. interest rates or political turmoil over human rights could pose some headaches.
But overall they feel that China will make it work because it wants it to and needs to.

Farrell argued there was a winning equation -- the low wages and relatively inexpensive real estate in southern China coupled with the entrepreneurial skills of the Hong Kong Chinese and the colony's sophisticated infrastructure.
"If this was a separate nation, it would have the same critical mass as France. We are talking about a significant economic force," he said.
Farrell, like other fund managers, fears that real estate shortages in Hong Kong itself could be a problem. "The supply on the horizon is not awfully good," he said.
"Politicians in North America and Europe will also seek to use trade as a method to beat the Chinese over the head over human rights," he forecast.
Richard Murckart, investment director at Edinburgh Fund Managers, adopted an equally upbeat position -- but also cautioned about soaring property prices.

"There are a lot of concerns and we have seen quite a few mutterings on the subject of property. They are trying to put a lid on it. Because of that, you have good days and bad days on the market," he said.

He forecast: "It won't be in a straight line and there will be some major hiccoughs. There will be challenges to the basic law (on the governing of Hong Kong) in the first six months but in general Hong Kong is a good place to invest."
Chinese self-interest is also a powerful motivation, Murckart argues.
"At the end of the day they know it is their lifeline for the next five to 10 years until they can establish alternative routes like Shanghai," he said.
Hong Kong could also require a delicate balancing act by Beijing's leaders.
"There is a playoff between the international world being satisfied that life goes on and the Chinese domestic scene being convinced Hong Kong is not being treated specially," he said.
"Asia is a risk worth taking and China is a great place to invest as long as you have the long time frame. A three to five year view will produce some wonderful returns," he prophesied.
Dudley Lord of Axa Equity and Law Investment is the first to admit there will be troughs and peaks.
"The market did have a dip at the time U.S. interest rates rose. But local liquidity is strong and the market has been at an all-time high," he said.
Lord argued that economic confidence is soundly based in Hong Kong.
"At the moment there is a degree of equanimity. It is sounder in economic terms than the rest of Asia which has poor export markets and overblown property markets."
And he concluded with a blunt assessment of how Communist China views one of the most successful capitalist money-making machines in the world.
"They don't understand how it works so they don't want to tinker with it."
